title.en: The greedy good-doers and the poet's pain

hook.en: Sometimes the people who claim to help us take away our freedom instead. Frost has sharp words for the officials who plan to improve the lives of the poor.

objectives.en: Explain the plan of the so-called good-doers
Interpret the oxymorons used for them
Understand the poet's personal anguish at the end

narration.en: Sometimes the people who claim to help us take away our freedom instead. Frost has sharp words for the officials who plan to improve the lives of the poor.

body.en: Frost mentions news that the poor will be bought out of their land and moved into villages near a theatre and a store, where they will not have to think for themselves. He calls the planners greedy good-doers and beneficent beasts of prey: they appear kind but are really selfish exploiters. Their benefits are meant to soothe the poor out of their wits.

text.en: Bringing a theatre and a store nearby
Buy the poor out of their land
Move them where they need not think
Lull them out of their wits
Prey on them for their own gain

explanation.en: Frost's oxymorons for the planners show the gap between their kind looks and their selfish aims.

body.en: The poet says he can hardly bear the thought of the sellers' unending wait. In a dark moment he feels it would be kinder to put them out of their pain at one stroke. But he immediately turns the question on himself: how would he like to be put out of his own pain? The ending shows deep empathy, not cruelty.

problem.en: Who are the "greedy good-doers" and why does the poet criticise them?

steps.en: Identify them: planners and officials who claim to help the rural poor.
Describe their plan: buy out the poor and move them near theatres and stores.
Explain the oxymoron: they look kind but act out of greed.
Conclude: their help takes away the freedom and self-respect of the poor.

answer.en: They are planners and officials who claim to help the poor. They buy out the farmers and move them to villages near theatres and stores, forcing benefits that dull their minds. Frost calls them greedy good-doers because their kindness hides selfish motives and robs the poor of freedom.
